historical_timeline.summary: Born at Park House, near Sandringham, Norfolk.
Married at St Paul's Cathedral, London.
Panorama interview broadcast, in which she spoke of bulimia, post-natal depression, and self-injury.
Died in Paris after a car crash.
BBC-commissioned inquiry found the interview had been obtained by deceit.

claims.statement: She was born The Honourable Diana Frances Spencer on 1 July 1961 at Park House, near Sandringham in Norfolk, England.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Spencer is her birth surname, used for the coded family name.

claims.statement: On 29 July 1981 she married the Prince of Wales at St Paul's Cathedral in London.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context only. The modern episode gives no role to her former husband, her children, or any other living person.

claims.statement: During her marriage she was president or patron of more than 100 charities, and she drew attention to homelessness, disability, children's causes, and HIV/AIDS.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her charity work anchors the modern work history.

claims.statement: She and the Prince of Wales separated in December 1992 and divorced on 28 August 1996.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; context only.

claims.statement: In an interview broadcast on the BBC's Panorama programme on 20 November 1995, she said that she had had bulimia for a number of years, calling it "a secret disease" that you inflict upon yourself "because your self-esteem is at a low ebb"; asked how long it went on, she said "a long time", a little more than two or three years, and "I'm free of it now".
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account, given after the index date. It anchors the modern episode of bulimia nervosa; the frequency, findings and treatment in the modern episode are synthetic.

source_links.locator: broadcast November 20, 1995; "I had bulimia for a number of years"

claims.statement: In the same interview she said that with bulimia "you fill your stomach up four or five times a day" and that "it gives you a feeling of comfort"; that it "was a symptom of what was going on in my marriage"; and that "when you have bulimia you're very ashamed of yourself", so you do not discuss it with people.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own words, recorded as history. The modern episode does not repeat her account of her marriage and gives no role to any real person.

source_links.locator: "It was a symptom of what was going on in my marriage"

claims.statement: In the same interview she said that she had been unwell with post-natal depression, "which no one ever discusses".
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account of depression, recorded briefly as history; the modern mood findings are synthetic.

claims.statement: In the same interview she said that at a time of great distress she had hurt her arms and legs: "You have so much pain inside yourself that you try and hurt yourself on the outside".
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account, recorded briefly as history only. The modern safety assessment notes past self-injury only as part of this history.

source_links.locator: had deliberately done something to her arms and legs

claims.statement: In May 2021 an independent inquiry commissioned by the BBC and led by Lord Dyson found that the 1995 interview had been obtained by deceit, in serious breach of the BBC's producer guidelines; the BBC accepted the findings in full and apologized.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Bears on how the interview was obtained, not on the words she spoke in it; recorded because the case relies on the interview.

claims.statement: She died in Paris on 31 August 1997 after a car crash.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Respectful, unhurried primary care for a 28-year-old woman who asks for help with bulimia nervosa she has hidden for years: a structured eating-disorder assessment (SCOFF and EDE-Q) and DSM-5-TR severity grading; a medical risk assessment for purging (orthostatic vital signs, potassium, magnesium, phosphate and bicarbonate, an ECG with the QTc, and the parotid, dental and skin findings of vomiting), with oral potassium replacement and clear thresholds for a higher level of care; eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) as first-line treatment with fluoxetine 60 mg daily, the medicine with the best evidence; nutrition built on regular eating; dental protection; measurement-based care for co-occurring depression; and a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline reviewed at every visit, on the APA 2023 eating disorders guideline, NICE NG69, and the CMID depression monograph.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient visit at her own request for binge eating and vomiting: eating-disorder assessment, medical risk assessment, low potassium, mood, and safety planning
One-week review: potassium recheck and eating disorders psychiatry consultation
Five-week review: potassium and ECG on fluoxetine 60 mg, CBT-E progress, mood, and safety
Three-month review: binge and purge frequency, electrolytes, dental care, mood, and safety
End-of-treatment review after 20 weeks of CBT-E: remission, relapse prevention, and continuing fluoxetine

problems.display: Bulimia nervosa, severe: recurrent binge eating, each time with self-induced vomiting, averaging about ten episodes a week for about three years, hidden from everyone; self-worth tied closely to body shape and weight; no laxatives, diuretics, diet pills, or excessive exercise. SCOFF 4 of 5; EDE-Q global score 3.9. Findings: bilateral parotid enlargement, enamel erosion on the inner surfaces of the upper front teeth, calluses on the backs of two knuckles of the right hand, a pulse rise of 22 per minute on standing, low potassium and chloride with a raised bicarbonate, and a raised amylase; BMI 19.3. Synthetic modern episode linked to her own public account of bulimia

hpi.narrative: Ms. Spencer returns one week after her first visit and is seen by Dr. Rosenthal, the eating disorders psychiatrist, on the same day. She has taken potassium chloride 20 mEq twice daily without stomach upset. She has kept the self-monitoring record she was given: seven episodes of binge eating with vomiting this week, from about ten, and breakfast on three days. She has met the dietitian once. She has had no palpitations, cramps, weakness, dizziness, or blood in the vomit. Her mood is still low and she is tired, but she says that telling someone has been a relief. She has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

documentation.chief_complaint: Five-week review: potassium and ECG on fluoxetine 60 mg, CBT-E progress, mood, and safety

hpi.narrative: Ms. Spencer returns four weeks after the consultation. She has had seven CBT-E sessions, twice a week, and keeps her self-monitoring record every day. Binge eating with vomiting has fallen to about three times a week, and she eats breakfast and lunch on four or five days a week. She took fluoxetine 20 mg for a week, 40 mg for a week, and has taken 60 mg each morning for two weeks. She had mild nausea in the first week, which passed; she sleeps well and has had no agitation or restlessness. The nurse's phone check ten days after the start found no concerns. She has taken potassium chloride twice daily. She has not booked a dental examination. Her mood is better and she has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

assessment.assessment: She meets the DSM-5-TR criteria: recurrent binge eating with a sense of loss of control, recurrent self-induced vomiting to prevent weight gain, both at least weekly for more than three months, and self-evaluation unduly shaped by weight and shape, without the low weight of anorexia nervosa. With about seven to ten compensatory episodes a week it is severe. Outpatient care is safe: potassium has risen to 3.6 mmol/L on oral replacement, the QTc is below 460 ms, she has not fainted, and the pulse rise on standing is modest. Because the illness is severe and has lasted years, eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-E) is a better choice than guided self-help. Fluoxetine 60 mg daily has the most evidence in bulimia nervosa and also treats her depression, so it should start now rather than after six weeks of psychotherapy alone. Bupropion should be avoided because of the risk of seizures in bulimia nervosa

A moderate depressive episode, recurrent given the earlier depression after childbirth. It often improves as bingeing and vomiting settle; fluoxetine treats both. Her risk of self-harm is higher with both conditions, so the safety plan should be reviewed at every visit, especially in the first weeks of fluoxetine
